summary: Describes Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA), IPv6 addresses whose interface identifier is a hash of a public key and other parameters. This binds the key to the address, which can be verified by recomputing the hash. It is used in Secure Neighbor Discovery.

plainLanguage.summary: A Cryptographically Generated Address (CGA) links an IPv6 address to a public key through a hash. A receiver can recompute the hash to check the link, then verify a message signed with the matching private key.

questions: what is a cryptographically generated address
how does cga work in ipv6
what is the cga sec parameter
subtitle: IPv6 addresses whose interface identifier is derived from a public key and related parameters.

tldr.problem: Secure Neighbor Discovery needs a way to bind an IPv6 address to a public key without relying on a certification authority or other security infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: A Cryptographically Generated Address uses a hash of a public key and auxiliary parameters to form its interface identifier. A verifier recomputes the hashes and can then verify messages signed with the matching private key.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3972 defines CGA generation, verification and signatures for SEND. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4581 and RFC 4982.

today: RFC 3972 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 4581 and RFC 4982 as updates, and lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Binding a Public Key to an Address
sections.content:
RFC 3972 defines a method for associating a public key with an IPv6 address for Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND). The rightmost 64 bits of the address, called the Interface Identifier, are generated from a cryptographic hash of the public key and auxiliary parameters.

The address owner can use the matching private key to sign messages. A verifier needs the address, public key and parameters to check the association, then can verify messages signed by the private key.

A CGA is not certified. Anyone can create a new CGA using a subnet prefix and a public key, but an attacker cannot use a different key to create signed messages that appear to come from the owner of an existing CGA.
sections.plainLanguage: A CGA links an IPv6 address to a public key using a hash. The matching private key can sign messages from that address, and others can check the link without using a certification authority.

sections.title: The Address and Security Parameter
sections.content:
A CGA has a 64-bit subnet prefix followed by a 64-bit Interface Identifier. Its three-bit security parameter, Sec, is stored in the three leftmost bits of the Interface Identifier.

Two conditions define a valid CGA. First, Hash1 must match the Interface Identifier except for the security-parameter bits and the two specified address bits. Second, the leftmost 16*Sec bits of Hash2 must be zero.

Sec ranges from 0 to 7. A higher value requires more leading zero bits in Hash2, increasing the work to generate a matching address and to search for a match.
sections.plainLanguage: The Interface Identifier contains part of the address's hash and a small security setting called Sec. A higher Sec value requires more zero bits in a second hash.

sections.title: CGA Parameters and Hashes
sections.content:
The CGA Parameters structure contains a 128-bit Modifier, a 64-bit Subnet Prefix, an 8-bit Collision Count, a public key and optional extension fields. The collision count MUST be 0, 1 or 2. The public key is a DER-encoded ASN.1 SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure.

Both Hash1 and Hash2 use SHA-1. Hash1 is the leftmost 64 bits of the hash over the full parameters structure. For Hash2, the same structure is hashed with the subnet prefix and collision count set to zero; Hash2 is the leftmost 112 bits.

Unrecognized extension fields are ignored as data by implementations, but remain part of the hash input. This allows verification to include fields added by later specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameters include a random modifier, the address prefix, a collision counter and the public key. Two SHA-1 results are computed from these fields to create and check the address.

sections.title: Generating and Checking an Address
sections.content:
To generate a CGA, choose a subnet prefix, public key and Sec value. Start with a random or pseudo-random 128-bit Modifier, then change it until Hash2 has the required leading zero bits. Compute Hash1, place Sec in the Interface Identifier and combine it with the subnet prefix.

If duplicate-address detection finds a collision, increment the Collision Count and recompute Hash1. After three collisions, stop and report an error. Generation with Sec set to 0 is deterministic and relatively fast; higher values require more search.

To verify the result, check that the Collision Count is allowed and that the parameter prefix matches the address prefix. Recompute Hash1 and Hash2, check the Interface Identifier and required zero bits, and stop at the first failed check. Verification always requires at most two SHA-1 computations.
sections.plainLanguage: Creating an address requires searching for a modifier that meets the Sec setting. Checking an address is quicker: recompute the hashes and compare them with the address and parameters.

sections.title: Signing Messages with a CGA
sections.content:
To sign a message, prepend a 128-bit type tag to the message and sign the combined data with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-1. The type tag distinguishes messages so that a signature from another protocol is not accepted as a SEND signature.

SEND defines the tag used for its signed messages. The tag is not carried in the SEND message because a verifier determines it from the ICMP message type.

A verifier first verifies the CGA, then verifies the signature using the public key in the CGA Parameters. It MUST accept the signature as authentic only when both checks succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender signs the message together with a type tag. A receiver accepts it only after the address binding and the message signature both verify.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
CGAs aim to prevent an attacker from taking over an existing IPv6 address. Impersonation would require a hash collision. However, the address is not certified, and the RFC defines no way to prove that an address is not a CGA.

The security parameter increases the work needed to generate an address and to search for a matching hash, while verification cost remains constant. The RFC says Sec values between 0 and 2 are sufficient for most IPv6 nodes at the time it was written. It also specifies a minimum RSA key length of 384 bits for SEND, while warning that such short keys are not suitable for strong authentication or secrecy.

Changing the random Modifier can produce multiple addresses and support pseudonymity, but a public key revealed in signed messages can link those addresses. A host seeking that privacy also needs to change keys. A CGA signing key MUST be used only for signing, not encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: CGAs make it difficult to impersonate an existing address, but they do not certify who owns a new address. Changing the modifier and key can reduce address linkability, while the Sec setting changes generation effort.

viz.caption: FIELDS IN THE CGA PARAMETERS STRUCTURE

items.title: Modifier
items.text: A 128-bit value used in the hash search and to add randomness.

items.title: Collision Count
items.text: An 8-bit value that MUST be 0, 1 or 2.

items.title: Extension Fields
items.text: Optional fields included in both hash inputs.

viz.caption: THE TWO CONDITIONS THAT DEFINE A CGA

data.title: CGA hash checks
data.code:
Hash1 & Mask1 == interface identifier & Mask1
Hash2 & Mask2 == 0

The leftmost 16*Sec bits of Hash2 must be zero.
